useCases.description: Project risks are identified reactively rather than proactively. Cost, schedule, quality, and safety issues are often only detected after they have already caused delays or rework, rather than being predicted and prevented early.

Design coordination issues are found late in the process. Cross-disciplinary clashes between architectural, structural, and MEP systems are often only discovered during construction, leading to costly rework and schedule delays.

Manual site‑progress reporting is subjective and delayed. Relying on walkthroughs and subcontractor self‑reports causes inaccurate tracking. Deviations between planned and actual work, subcontractor under‑performance and material gaps are only spotted after downstream project delays occur.

Subcontractor accountability is hard to enforce. Without objective, visual evidence of work completed, it is difficult to hold trade partners accountable for delays or quality issues, leading to disputes and claims.

As-built documentation is incomplete and outdated. Construction progress imagery is not systematically captured and linked to BIM models, making handover documentation unreliable for future facility management and renovation.

Manual processing dominates payment validation and periodic financial reporting. Teams manually cross-check pay applications against contracts, valuation schedules and change orders, and extract scattered cross-system data to build performance, cash flow and productivity spreadsheets, creating heavy admin burden, human errors, overpayment risks and compliance gaps.

Final account settlement is complex and time-consuming. Reconciling all changes, claims, and payments at project closeout requires gathering data from multiple systems and manual verification, delaying final payments and project closure.

Financial data is siloed across different systems. Project financials, ERP data, HR systems, and operational data are in separate platforms, making it hard to get a unified view of project performance and profitability.

Financial decision support for project teams is limited. Project managers lack real-time, data-driven insights into project financial health, relying instead on periodic reports that are outdated by the time they arrive.

MEP conceptual sizing, detailed routing design and tender documentation creation rely heavily on slow, manual repetitive engineering work. Heavy reliance on senior engineers extends design timelines, creates design bottlenecks, limits design alternative exploration and introduces inconsistent tender data.
useCases.aiValue: Autonomous MEP Design & Tender Output Automation

useCases.description: Design coordination requires iterative manual clash detection. Engineers spend significant time resolving clashes between disciplines, with each iteration taking days or weeks to complete.
There is a global shortage of experienced MEP engineers. Engineering firms struggle to find and retain qualified staff, limiting their capacity to take on projects and driving up costs for clients.

MEP designs often have coordination issues that are found late. Clashes between different MEP disciplines and with structural elements are typically discovered during construction, causing costly rework and delays.

Firms cannot easily encode and reuse institutional engineering knowledge. Each engineer designs differently based on their experience, and there is no systematic way to capture and standardize best practices across the organization.

MEP design optimization for energy efficiency is complex. Balancing system performance, energy consumption, and material cost requires sophisticated analysis that is often skipped due to time and resource constraints.

Project teams lack early visibility into potential risks that could derail projects. Risks related to delays, cost overruns, and construction errors are not systematically identified and quantified during the feasibility phase, leading to go/no-go decisions based on incomplete information.

Project data is siloed across SharePoint, construction cloud platforms, and other systems. Risk-relevant information is scattered across documents, schedules, and communications, making it impossible to get a holistic view of project risk in real time.

Risk assessment during bidding is subjective and inconsistent. Different team members evaluate risk differently based on experience, and there is no standardized, data-driven approach to quantifying risk exposure across bid options.

Unplanned field issues lack automated risk-level triage, leading to equal resource investment on minor and high-impact problems. Change orders trigger heavy cost overruns and disputes; teams cannot forecast schedule & budget impacts of variations or benchmark live project risk profiles against historical records.
